extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political philosophy, statesmen, and policymakers
extracted.subtask_short: preserving governments and causes of revolution
extracted.subtask_description: Analyze the causes that produce revolutions in different constitutions (democracy, oligarchy, aristocracy, monarchy) and the practical measures and qualifications recommended to preserve stable government. Extract principles for prevention, organization, and selection of magistrates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of Sedition: approaching equality between opposed parts
rubrics_metrics.description: A state is liable to commotions when those parts of it which seem to be opposite to each other approach to an equality (e.g., the rich and the common people), so that the middle part is insignificant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When formerly one party is evidently stronger the weaker will not hazard danger; but when inequality diminishes, sedition becomes likely. This explains many historical revolutions described (general principle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of revolution: violence or fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: Revolutions are brought about in two ways, either by violence or by fraud (deception leading to willing consent followed by force, or persuasion followed by consent to be governed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the four hundred deceiving people about Persian support; demagogues persuading then imposing changes. Both routes should be watched for in assessing risk of regime change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demagogues as primary threat in democracies
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracies are most subject to revolutions from the dishonesty of their demagogues, who inform against men of property or set the people against the wealthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practices include bribery, distributing gifts, accusing notables to drive them into combination against the people. Historical examples: Cos, Rhodes, Heraclea, Megara, Cume; anti-pattern: demagogue-general who uses military power to establish tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequence of demagogues who are also military leaders
rubrics_metrics.description: When the same person is both demagogue and general, democracies were formerly changed into tyrannies (because such figures could seize power).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Less common when oratory, not military command, is the demagogue's power. Historical examples: Pisistratus, Theagenes, Dionysius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of regulated census/election leads to constitutional change
rubrics_metrics.description: A government will alter from its ancient democratic form into a new one if there is no census to regulate the election of magistrates; elections by the mass leave room for demagogues to make the people superior to the laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preventive measure recommended: elect magistrates by tribes (or other intermediate bodies) rather than by the people at large.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oligarchic instability from mistreatment/exclusion of people
rubrics_metrics.description: Oligarchies are liable to revolution when the excluded (those with no share in administration) are ill used or repeatedly denied access to power, provoking disputes until they gain admission or overthrow the few.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Massilia, Ister, Heraclea, where non-participants raised disputes until admitted; remedy: allow broader participation or checks to reduce grievance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal demagogues and factionalism within oligarchies
rubrics_metrics.description: Oligarchies suffer revolutions from demagogues who flatter either the few in power or the people (two sorts), and from quarrels among ruling families or demagogues themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Charicles, Phrynichus; risk increased when magistrates are chosen by soldiers or people rather than self-selection by rulers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration of oligarchic power (creating sub-oligarchies) causes revolt
rubrics_metrics.description: An oligarchy is endangered when it creates a smaller ruling body under it (management in few hands, life-senates, nepotistic elections), concentrating supreme power and provoking opposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Elis with a senate of ninety; anti-pattern: preserving power within families like Lacedemonian senators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on mercenaries and military leaders produces tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: In war and peace oligarchies that distrust citizens and hire mercenaries may empower generals or commanders who can assume tyranny or become arbiters and masters of the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Timophanes at Corinth; Simos and the Aleuadae at Larissa; remedy: involve citizens in defense and command or reduce mercenary dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oligarchic instability from luxury and corruption of nobles
rubrics_metrics.description: When the nobility spend fortunes on luxury they become prone to supporting innovations or tyranny, inciting commotions or facilitating foreign-backed changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Hypparinus supporting Dionysius; Cleotimus creating quarrels by settling colonies; anti-pattern: nobles squandering fortunes and provoking unrest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seditions can arise from ordinary civic disputes (lawsuits, marriages, punishments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common legal or personal conflicts (e.g., quarrels over law-suits, marriages, punishments illegally executed) can trigger seditions in oligarchies and other regimes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Heraclea, Thebes; implication: fair, lawful adjudication and restraint in punishments reduce this risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Census drift: changes in wealth relative to fixed census destabilize regime
rubrics_metrics.description: If the census remains fixed while the quantity of money or general wealth changes, the class eligible for government shifts, turning oligarchies into free states or democracies and vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remedy: periodically take account of total wealth and legally extend or contract the census (yearly in small cities, every 3–5 years in larger ones).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve constitution by preventing small illegalities (watch small changes)
rubrics_metrics.description: In well-tempered governments, nothing should be done contrary to law, especially matters of small consequence; small repeated illegalities erode the constitution slowly and secretly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: small household expenses consume income; first vigilance is required; political implication: check minor infractions before they accumulate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't trust false pretences and deceivers
rubrics_metrics.description: No credit should be given to those who endeavour to deceive the people with false pretences, since they will be confuted by facts and cause corruption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political actors should expose false claims and prevent rulers or demagogues from deceiving populace about external support or benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include outsiders in administration and don't injure those who lack office
rubrics_metrics.description: Magistrates should avoid injuring those not in power and should introduce consequential persons among them into office, to reduce grievances and broaden support for the constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practices: avoid confiscations, banishments; allow rotation and inclusion of capable citizens into magistracies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of treatment among those in power
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who have parts in the management of public affairs should behave to each other upon an equality to prevent envy, faction, and corruption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rule: limit tenure lengths (example: no one to continue in office longer than six months where many share administration) and conferring moderate honours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit accumulation of rank and power; moderate honours
rubrics_metrics.description: A general maxim: do not let any one acquire a rank far superior to the rest of the community; confer moderate honours for continuance rather than great ones for a short time, and if honors must be rescinded, do it gradually and by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If someone has excess power or fortune contrive their departure; this reduces the chance of tyranny arising from inequality of influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Officer to inspect manners and guard against innovators
rubrics_metrics.description: Appoint an officer to inspect citizens' manners and ensure they are not contrary to the genius of the state; guard particularly against the most prosperous who promote innovations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: to preserve civic mores aligned with constitution; practical anti-corruption and cultural policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend classes and increase middle rank to reduce inequality-driven seditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Oppose men of account to common people, the poor to the rich, and blend both into one body; increase numbers in the middle rank to prevent seditions arising from inequality of condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies: promote institutions and offices that enlarge the middle class and avoid extreme concentrations of property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent venality in public servants; transparency of public accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Prevent those employed by the public from being venal (especially in oligarchies); deliver public money openly to the city and deposit copies of accounts across divisions to prevent embezzlement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency and public oversight; reward honest magistrates with honours even if offices are unpaid to discourage corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make public office unprofitable to harmonize rich and poor
rubrics_metrics.description: If public office brings no profit, both rich and poor will be satisfied: the poor will not vie for office for gain, and the rich will take office for honour, blending democratic and aristocratic aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical measure: remove emoluments from offices; instead provide non-monetary honours for good service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect property in democracies and provide gainful employments in oligarchies
rubrics_metrics.description: In democracies protect the rich from illicit division of lands or unperceivable erosion of property; in oligarchies take care of the poor by allotting gainful public employments and equalizing inheritance rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: prevent unnecessary public entertainments that squander resources; in oligarchies make punishment for insulting the poor severer and restrict number of estates per person to prevent extremes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fill principal offices by those best qualified
rubrics_metrics.description: All principal offices in the state should be filled only by those best qualified to discharge them (meritocratic principle), balancing ability, affection for constitution, and virtue appropriate to the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection rules vary by office: prefer courage for generals, virtue/prudence for financial or custodial offices. Consider which quality the generality possesses more when choosing among imperfect candidates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three qualifications for top magistrates
rubrics_metrics.description: The three necessary qualifications for those who fill the first departments in government: (1) affection for the established constitution; (2) abilities completely equal to the business of their office; (3) virtue and justice corresponding to the nature of that particular state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If all three don't exist in one person, choose based on which quality the community lacks more; e.g., prioritise courage in generals because it is rarer, prioritise virtue in guardians of state/finances because prudence is critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve a mean and avoid extremes
rubrics_metrics.description: Preserve a mean: many things seemingly favourable to a democracy or an oligarchy destroy them when carried to excess; excesses change the form of government entirely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislators and politicians should know what preserves and destroys a constitution; avoid policies that create total equality of circumstances or extreme inequality of honors/power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educate children for the constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Education of citizens is the chief support of the constitution: children must be brought up in the principles of the established constitution so the laws and institutions can function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education should form citizens able to conduct either democracy or oligarchy as required; avoid raising magistrates' children in luxury and the poor's children in excessive hardship to prevent innovation-seeking cohorts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper definition and limits of liberty in democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: In democracy freedom does not mean every one doing as they please; subjection to government is protection not slavery; demagogues must not make the people superior to the laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civic education and legal constraints should define liberty properly and restrain demagogues from undermining rule of law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oaths and official language should bind rulers to not injure the people
rubrics_metrics.description: Oaths in oligarchies should assert non-injury to the people rather than promising hostility to them (i.e., officials should swear to avoid harming the populace).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changing the form of official oaths can reduce institutional bias against the people and lower resentment that causes revolutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monarchical stability: king vs tyrant distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: A kingdom (king) should protect property and common good, drawing rulers from virtue, family, benefaction; a tyranny arises from demagogues or power exceedance and seeks wealth and pleasure, using foreign guards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that tyrannies combine defects of democracy and oligarchy; preserve monarchy by avoiding contempt, injustice, and excessive accumulation of honors/wealth by ruler; guards should be citizens not foreigners.
